subsubtopic: ZONING REGULATIONS AFFECTING FARMERS' SILOS AT CHATHAM AND HAMILTON, ONT.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me tell you a story about two farm silos. One is located in the flight path at the Chatham, Ontario, airport. The other silo stands in the flight path at Mount Hope, in my riding, where Hamilton Civic Airport is currently undergoing expansion.
My constituent, Mr. Joseph Popper, last year received authorization from Transport Canada and the Municipality of Glanbrook to erect a silo in accordance with Hamilton airport zoning and height restrictions. Several months later the Department of Public Works claimed that Joe Popper's silo violates the height in feet above mean sea level. Although local pilots have indicated no problems or any incidents in the area, Mr. Popper has now been ordered to take immediate action to remove about 10 feet off the top of the silo. That would mean a very heavy financial burden for the Poppers, who are understandably upset that they had acted in accordance with Transport Canada and the Municipality of Glanbrook height regulations in the first place.
We switch you to the controversial silo at Chatham, Mr. Speaker. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Axworthy) has agreed to solve that problem after meeting with the Hon. Member for Kent (Mr. Bossy) and the Mayor of Chatham, along with Transport Canada officials.
Meanwhile, at Mount Hope, my office, Glanbrook Mayor Don Weylie, and Joe Popper, have yet to hear from Transport Canada, despite repeated attempts during the past several weeks to work out a compromise similar to Chatham airport.
Farm silos are not porkbarrels. After what we have been through this week about government favouritism toward Liberal ridings, I sincerely hope the Minister of Transport will rise above treating these situations as first and second class silos.

subsubtopic: TAX ON TIPS EARNED BY WAITERS AND WAITRESSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are 600,000 Canadians who work as waiters or waitresses throughout Canada. Most of them receive minimum wage, or a little more, and supplement their low wages with the tips they receive.
Recently Revenue Canada has begun to enforce a rule that they must pay income tax, not just on their wage but on their total income of wage and tips. However, when they pay their unemployment insurance premiums and Canada Pension Plan, it is done on the basis of the lower wage. When they are unemployed they receive unemployment insurance benefits at the lower rate, and when they qualify for Canada Pension they will get it at the lower rate.
I call on the Government to change the laws and regulations so that, if these people must pay income tax on their total income, they will also receive benefits based on their total income.

subsubtopic: LAY-OFFS AT BLACK AND DECKER PLANT IN BROCKVILLE, ONT.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in his Budget Speech a week ago the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) stood in this House and whetted our appetites with proud promises of lasting economic recovery and sound fiscal policies. He said:
In my April Budget, my goal was to secure the recovery. That goal has been met.
I would ask the Minister how can he justify that statement when just last Friday 110 employees were laid off at Black and Decker in Brockville, Ontario. This is a responsible, sound firm, that has provided 700 local residents with secure employment for over 25 years.
In announcing these lay-offs, the company president stated the signs of economic recovery last spring had caused them to anticipate a higher volume of sales than actually materialized when the economy failed to recover as the Minister predicted in his April Budget.
The Government has failed these employees with its promises to secure economic recovery and job stabilization. Government spending grew almost 10 per cent last year, well over its own six and five guidelines imposed on Canadians to reduce inflation. The message was obviously "Do as I say, not as I do".
The Finance Minister's Budget Speech, full of rhetoric and encouragement, held little for these recently unemployed Canadians in my riding.

subsubtopic: BUDGET OF SOCIAL SCIENCES AND HUMANITIES RESEARCH COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the self-congratulatory press release of the Department of Communications of February 16, 1984, misleads the Canadian public. It suggests that the base budget of the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council will increase by $2 million to almost $59 million in the financial year 1984-1985. In fact the budget of the Research Council will be substantially reduced. A previous allocation of $5.9 million for Canadian studies will not be renewed. The Government's magic arithmetic, as the Canadian Association of University Teachers calls it, gives the Council an increase of $2 million, but really it loses $1.2 million.
This sleight-of-hand is taking place at a time when millions of dollars are available at the whims of Liberal MPs, but post-secondary education support is being attacked under the six and five formula.
The Social Science Federation of Canada affirms that most major problems are both social and economic. More, not less, research is needed. High technology is impacting on the job market, especially for women. Prostitution, pornography, and visible minorities, are all being studied by separate and expensive commissions. Why, I ask, is the Government setting up costly parallel mechanisms for research, and refusing to introduce a five-year plan for research in the social sciences and humanities?

I acknowledge, Mr. Speaker, that the view in some areas of western Canada is different. It is neither pernicious nor benighted. It is simply different. It is different because the evolution of western Canada did not in some very important respects parallel the evolution in the east.
Vast waves of courageous immigrants from the Ukraine, Central Europe and elsewhere arrived to cause the Prairies to blossom and grow. Their sense of sacrifice and their unremitting commitment to the soil gave life to western Canada. Though different in background, they found in western Canada common ground in language. English became the quasi-universal instrument of communication. In many ways, in many important ways it became a unifying force among people of remarkably diverse backgrounds.
That precious and fragile dimension of linguistic duality which Macdonald and Cartier saw as an indispensable characteristic of nationhood was submerged by growing demographic realities of the new west. The country grew; the English language became more dominant and ultimately more pervasive. This was the silent and the inexorable toll of history. In my judgment, it emerged less through contrivance than through the irresistible effect of overwhelming numbers. Large groups of Germans, Ukrainians, Poles, Swedes and Icelanders have made the Prairies home.
But what of the small group of Franco-Manitobans who were there at the beginning as one of the founding partners of the dual linguistic dimension of Canada? They were there with rights and obligations, establishing the unique beachhead for Canada. They would later be joined by so many others of whom I have spoken who opted for the English-speaking side
of our unique dual dimension. But the linguistic rights of Franco-Manitobans were not submerged. They were removed. They were removed by a wilful act of the legislature in violation of a historic understanding. Today, Mr. Speaker, we ask simply that these rights be returned.

It is a legitime concern which all of us as parents can understand. But it is not the real issue in the Province of Manitoba.
The legislation before that legislature is limited. It limits French language services to areas where the population warrants those services. It limits the use of those services in government offices. I say to all Canadians that it does not provide complete protection and complete use of services to the Francophone minority in Manitoba, but it does recognize the historic right of that population and that where there is a French speaking community, there should be services for those people.
The proposals in Manitoba provide adequate safeguards for both the minority and the majority. That is important for all of us to understand, important for all Manitobans to understand. I am a Manitoban who speaks only English. I am learning French but it is a slow process for me. I represent a riding where there are two official languages, English and Cree. In my riding 30 per cent of the population speak Cree. They are
Official Languages
not affected in a positive way by this legislation, but they are people who can understand that in Canada we are not just English and French; we are not just English, French and Ukrainian; we are not just English, French, Ukrainian and German. We are a mosaic, not a melting pot. In Canada, as in Manitoba, we must respect that fact. We must respect the concerns and the aspirations of the Ukrainian population, the concerns of the Mennonite population, indeed the concerns of all segments of our population. In the Manitoba Legislature that is what is being attempted, and both I and my caucus support it not only on historic grounds but because it is the right thing to do in Canada; it is the right thing to do in the Province of Manitoba.

subtopic: RESOLUTION ON FRENCH LANGUAGE RIGHTS IN MANITOBA
speechtext:
Since 1870 we have had protection in our Constitution in Manitoba for the French and English fact. In 1870 the French-speaking native population was the majority. Louis Riel, as a result of a rebellion, negotiated with the Government of Canada for the protection of both English and French. That is a proud part of our history and we should all recognize that. Now that the English are the majority, now that other cultural and linguistic groups have surpassed the French, we should also show the tolerance of Riel. We should recognize that there are some services, some basic rights, for a group which granted the minority of that day, the English, those rights.
We in this nation are anything but monolithic. But if the majority in our nation ever decides that it is going to use its power as some in the Province of Manitoba are presently trying to do, if they are going to use that power on the French-speaking population of Manitoba with its constitutional guarantee which has been upheld by the Supreme Court of Canada, then, Mr. Speaker, no Canadian is safe; no religious minority is safe, no linguistic minority is safe, no individual or group of individuals with different beliefs from the majority is safe in this country.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mark MacGuigan (Minister of Justice) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
that Bill C-10, an Act to amend the Divorce Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, to rise to support second reading of amendments to the Divorce Act, the first amendments since 1968 and, in fact, the most fundammental we have ever had to our law of divorce in Canada, is not a happy task. It is, rather, an onerous and painful duty. I believe the subject of marriage breakdown is one which many people in Canada would wish not to have to deal with. Indeed, we all wish that the reality in our country was not such that this is a matter which we are now required to consider. We are told that the estimate is that there is about a 40 per cent chance for any marriage entered into now to end in divorce.

Mr. Speaker, the concept of the family and the sacredness of marriage are deeply rooted in our society. As a government, we are entirely in favour of protecting and supporting this institution in Canada. For instance, our policies on the tax system, family allowances, the Canada Assistance Plan in relation to day-care and employment all indicate the Government's strong support for the institution of marriage and its preservation in Canada.
As for the causes of marriage breakdown, they are many: financial problems, urban overcrowding, housing shortages, increased mobility in our society owing to the search for employment and career development, changes in the traditional roles of men and women and finally, the emphasis on individual rights.
Mr. Speaker, marriage breakdown is a fact, and the Divorce Act is not intended as preventive but as curative legislation, aimed at organizing the legal status of people whose marriage has already broken down.
I also would like to make the point that the Divorce Act in its present form is destructive rather than constructive, and that it should be changed in order to promote as much as possible, reconciliation of the parties, in the hope of avoiding a divorce.

If this set of amendments to the law of divorce were likely to have the effect of undermining the institution of marriage in our society, we as a government would not be putting them forward. As 1 indicated, this law of divorce has to deal with a social fact. The social fact of marriage breakdown is occurring for broad social causes, for reason, entirely independent of the
February 24, 1984

laws of Canada. It may be true, indeed it is true, that the law regulates the number of divorces that take place each year in Canada, but it is not the law but rather social conditions that regulate and cause the number of marriage breakdowns which occur in our country. The role of the law is to deal with the social reality and the terrible cost in human pain and suffering which are involved in it.
As I will illustrate in the course of my remarks, it is the children more than any other single group who are the losers in marriage breakdown, in divorce. We would wish to have a law which would be so humanized that the children would suffer less than now is occurring under the law-as little, indeed, as our law can make possible.
Many people seem to have the idea that these proposals will make divorce easier to obtain in Canada. I categorically deny that interpretation, if by easier they mean quicker. This law, in fact, will make it slower, more difficult, for more than three-quarters of Canadians who now are obtaining divorces.
Statistics Canada tells us that in the years from 1969 to 1977, 75.8 per cent of divorce cases were completed through to decree absolute in less than 360 days, which is less than the period of one year which we are making the minimum possible for obtaining divorce under our amendments. In other words, three-quarters of the Canadians now obtaining divorces obtain them in less than the time we are proposing as the minimum time in this legislation. Because of the legislation, one-quarter of Canadians will be able to get their divorces more quickly but three-quarters will have to wait.
No, you are wrong.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The Hon. Member simply does not know the statistics.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. For the sake of orderly debate the Minister should be allowed to make his comments now and replies will follow.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I can tell Hon. Members that these statistics are available through Statistics Canada, and they refer to a considerable period of years. In case the Hon. Member is not aware of what is now happening in our courts, I can tell him that since this legislation was given First reading in the House I have spoken to groups of lawyers practising family law in many cities in Canada; in Toronto, Victoria, London, Windsor, Charlottetown and other centres. They showed massive support for this legislation because as lawyers they understand what is actually happening. I have heard of divorces being granted in five weeks, four weeks, three weeks, and in one case from the beginning of the divorce to decree absolute a total of only nine days. That is what the present law in Canada is bringing about.
We are going to require all of these people, without exception, to wait a minimum of a year. We believe that there has to be time for reconsideration and reconciliation. The law which we are proposing would encourage married couples to reflect on their decision to divorce. It would impose an obligation on
Divorce Act
those who counsel them to draw to their attention the mediatory facilities which exist. It would also change the law with respect to the reconciliation period so that there would no longer be only a single period of cohabitation for reconciliation during the running of the time for divorce. It would be possible to have any number of such periods of reconciliation up to a maximum of three months.
More important than even those points, Mr. Speaker, is our proposal to reduce the accusatory aspect of the divorce process to the absolute minimum. As Hon. Members know, the reason that most people who are now applying for divorces can get them in such a short time is that they are obtaining them on the basis of cause: adultery, physical cruelty, mental cruelty and so on. The legal necessity for alleging cause-and we fear sometimes even for fabricating cause-in order to obtain a divorce is a legal concept which imposes an atmosphere of confrontation on the parties. It can involve the children as pawns in the marriage breakup, and it can, as I am sure Hon. Members know, have the effect of having children called in on examinations for discovery to testify, for instance, that they saw their father beating their mother.
We already know, Mr. Speaker, as my earlier words indicated, that children in all divorces carry a sense of guilt that they were somehow unwittingly the cause of the marriage breakup. When the law adds to this natural psychological tendency by requiring there be accusation, and sometimes accusation piled on accusation and counter-accusation, it of course adds to the guilt that a child will feel, especially if the child has to testify to prove the existence of the cause of cruelty on which the divorce may be based.
There is a profound need, Mr. Speaker, for the humanization of our divorce system in Canada. That is the objective of the Government in this legislation. It is not to make divorce easier. In fact, it will not make divorce easier.
It will make divorce less expensive, I am happy to say, by the fact of enabling the provinces to adopt rules and procedures which will eliminate the making of the decree in open court. The expense of lawyers will diminish, it is our estimate, to a third or a half of the present billing. Therefore, there will certainly be a financial saving on the part of couples who are seeking divorce. It will, in addition to what I mentioned, make the process as healing and as mediating as I believe it is possible for the law to do.
Of course, in order for this to happen most effectively, as I will also indicate later, there are some other changes apart from the law of divorce which are also necessary, such as more facilities for mediation and conciliation in our country.

Before concluding this explanation of the Bill, Mr. Speaker, I would like to stress some of the proposed aspects of the reform which are more technical but none the less significant. The way things are now, three conditions are required before a petition for divorce can be filed before provincial courts: first, the petitioner must be a Canadian resident; second, one of the
1718

February 24, 1984
Divorce Act
two parties involved must have been a resident of the province for at least one year at the time of the petition; third, that same person must have been a resident of that same province for ten months. I intend to replace those three conditions by only one, namely that one of the parties must have resided for at least one year in the province where the petition is filed. That would simplify the issue and provide easier access to the courts.
Under the existing system, orders concerning alimony or child custody can be changed only by the court which has issued them. This rule may have serious consequences. For example, let us take the case of a couple whose divorce was granted in Toronto, one of the spouses now being in St. John's and the other in Calgary. Any order pertaining to alimony or child custody issued at the time of the divorce of that couple could be changed only by the Toronto court.
I intend to make the rule less stringent in that respect. Under the Bill, if both parties agree, a petition for any variation of the order pertaining to either question could be filed before any court. Should only one of the parties want to have the order changed, that party could apply before the court of his or her province, or that of the province where the other party resides. However, the court will always be free to turn down the petition should it feel that, under the circumstances, either party would be wronged.
The suggested amendments represent an in-depth review of the Divorce Act. In fact, such a review is long overdue. The proposed reform is based on a new approach not only to the grounds for divorce, but also to the whole divorce system. The procedure will be greatly simplified. As for the judicial rules concerning the determination of the effects of divorce, that is the rights and obligations of spouses as well as the rights of the children, they will be made more specific and more sensible.
This reform will have a direct impact on the welfare of an increasing number of Canadians.
There have been virtually no changes made to the Divorce Act in the past fifteen years. The principles on which it is based must be reexamined in the light of modern social trends. We need a more humane system for settling marital conflicts, a system which will be more effective and less distressing for those faced with the painful experience of divorce. We need a statute which will take the needs of people into greater consideration and which is more in agreement with the interests of society as a whole.
The reform project which I have just outlined will, I believe, allow us to fulfil all those objectives.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have no intention of taking all the time which would be available to me, but I would like to make one or two additional points with respect to the legislation and then review briefly some parallel initiatives.
In response to the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada in the case of Messier versus Lessard we have provided objectives for maintenance orders in the Bill. This is the first time there have been such objectives in the Divorce Act. The Supreme Court has now effectively required them. Even if it had not, they would be useful tools for the judiciary in deciding how to deal with the question of maintenance.
It is very important to note that the objectives set forth there are not absolute. There is obviously some overlapping. There are also key words in Clause 10 of the Bill. Those words are "in so far as is practicable". Those words govern each of the four objectives which follow.
With respect to children, we have for the first time set forth principles respecting children. It is important to note that this is put in terms of a right of the children; the children ought to have as much access to each of the spouses as the circumstances permit. That in particular is a very important statement of principle.
It should also not escape notice, Mr. Speaker, that for the first time we have provided for access by other parties to the children. In those comparatively rare cases where it was appropriate, this could mean that any person other than the parents could have the custody, care and upbringing of the children. It also includes access to the children. Of course, that would apply to the respective grandparents more than to any other group. This possible right of grandparents has long been overlooked by the law, so this is a very important change.
[DOT] (UlO)
Also important is the change which in the discretion of the court, allows the appointment of an advocate to represent the interests of the children. We have not laid down rules with respect to how this should be done, thinking it best to leave it to the discretion of the court to work out. Of course, there is discretion in the provinces to establish rules which may be relevant to all of these situations.
The provinces will have the discretion to decide how divorce actions will actually be handled, whether they will continue to be handled in open court or, if not in open court, whether they will continue to be dealt with by a judge. From what little I have heard on this point, the disposition of most provinces
February 24, 1984

seems to be to keep the involvement of the judges in the process but through some simpler procedure than decisions made in open court, as at present.
I also mentioned that I would like to deal with some parallel initiatives. Any Divorce Act, particularly in our federal state, is necessarily very limited legislation. It deals only with a very well defined territory. There are other initiatives which are necessary and we are taking those initiatives. 1 might mention that in his Budget the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) announced that the Canada Pension Plan would be improved to provide for mandatory credit splitting of Canada Pension Plan credits on marriage breakdown. As well, for all private pension plans under federal jurisdiction the Minister provides that there will be splitting of pensions between spouses in the case of marriage breakdown. I think those are important principles to have established.
We are also concerned about the fact that there presently are not adequate institutions or an adequate number of properly prepared people to assist in the very important process of conciliation and mediation in the case of marriage breakdown. If this can lead to reconciliation, of course, that's all the better; but even if it cannot lead to reconciliation it can lead to the easing of discussions over questions of custody and maintenance and therefore can be of great assistance.
It is my hope that some of the money that the provinces save on legal aid will be devoted by those provinces to trying to establish adequate systems of conciliation-mediation. We will be taking some initiatives in this area ourselves in order to show our concern about the development of a better system of mediation conciliation across Canada.
The final matter I wish to mention is, in some ways, the most important of all, though it is not in itself a matter for a Divorce Act. That is the matter of enforcement of ancillary orders, orders of maintenance and custody. This is another serious social problem.
It has been estimated that some 75 per cent of the maintenance orders in Canada are now in arrears. Spouses-I am afraid this is normally the husband-have been known to go to great lengths to escape the liability which the court has imposed on them at the time of divorce, by moving to other provinces or even by disappearing. All governments in Canada must do everything they can to deal with this problem.
As the House knows, since ancillary orders are registered as orders in provincial courts, this is a matter for the provinces primarily to deal with. They have the jurisdiction in this area. The only way I am aware that we could conceivably get federal jurisdiction is to use the Federal Court across the country as the court for divorce. However, the Federal Court is not generally accessible to people. I think it would not be as effective a system as the present one, even with all of its deficiencies.
Thus, I believe we are limited to proceeding with the present system or some variation of it in which the provinces have jurisdiction over these orders. We have had a federal-provincial study and a number of recommendations have been made
Divorce Act
to provinces and the federal Government. We have followed those recommendations in our divorce legislation to the limited extent that it is possible. For instance, we have provided for the possibility for easier variation of orders subsequent to their initially being obtained. We have also provided that it will be possible for a judge to require the party on whom maintenance payments fall to give security as well as to incur an obligation to pay on a monthly basis. This possibility of security-of course, in cases where the party with the responsibility has property against which the security can be made effective- will be a very effective new remedy.
Beyond that, it is important to try to move to what I would call a national enforcement network. It is only in this way that I believe we can really have greater success in the implementation of ancillary orders. In this respect, I was able to announce recently not only that the federal Government was prepared to agree to a national divorce registry and ways of making it effective through tracing and enforcement, but that the provinces now appear to be willing to go along in this direction as well.
Once again, I want to pay tribute to my colleague, the Minister responsible for the Status of Women (Mrs. Erola), and her departmental officers for their efforts in continuing to press for a national registry of maintenance and custody orders. Their efforts have helped in the very significant breakthrough that I think has been made in reviving the interest of the provinces in this kind of proposal and improvement of enforcement procedures generally. Officials from my Department and that of the status of women are now working together in studying the feasibility of establishing a national registry of custody and maintenance orders. I very much appreciate the contribution of my colleague and her officials.
I was able to tell the House recently that at a recent meeting of deputy attorneys general there was a general disposition to proceed with the establishment of such a registry. There will be a further meeting in this respect in March. I believe it is realistically possible to hope that even in this year we can achieve success in setting up such a registry. The Government of Canada is prepared to contribute its share. I think the operational costs would not be great but, of course, there obviously will be some start-up costs to which I would expect all governments would wish to contribute. The Government of Canada would certainly wish to be part of that because we want, so far as we can, to induce, lead and persuade the provinces that we really cannot go on any longer without establishing a national enforcement network.
As I mentioned, these parallel concerns are terribly important. They are not matters that can be resolved by divorce legislation but they are matters that are worth mentioning in the discussion of divorce legislation. They are certainly matters which are worth pursuing as objectives of national importance.
Within the divorce legislation itself, we have adopted a new approach. We have changed the basis of the law so that it will

February 24, 1984
Divorce Act
no longer be adversarial in this area of human difficulty, so that we will not add to natural difficulties, artificial problems created by an adversary system which, as we all know, is sometimes in all respects misused and abused.
The non-adversarial, no-fault basis which we are proposing for divorce will enable divorce to take place when marriage breakdown has already occurred with the least trauma possible. We have to support the institution of marriage in every way possible. When that institution has already ceased to function because marriage breakdown has occurred, as testified to by the witness of the parties themselves, we have to try and resolve the social problems without the addition of legal burdens that are in themselves unnecessary and are no longer related to the social conditions in which we find ourselves. That is the essence of what we are trying to do. It is to change the atmospherics of the divorce process so there can be a humanization of that process, one which can benefit all of the participants but especially the children whose interests, most of all, need to be protected. We believe this is very much in the interests of society.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, are there any provisions in the rules for questioning the Minister?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Not at this time. Under the rules this is not possible for the first three speakers.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to participate in this very important debate with respect to the first amendments we have had relating to divorce law in Canada for over 15 years.
Before I proceed with my remarks, I might be forgiven, after hearing the Minister in his remarks speak about the initiative taken on the part of the federal Government in the area of divorce reform, to observe that the Minister seems to be sending out different signals with respect to this legislation. When the legislation was introduced in the House and presented to the press in a formal press conference, as I recall the Minister referred to it at that time as a step forward toward a more efficient, faster and more facile method of obtaining divorce in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I never said faster.

The Minister confirms this. I just want to make sure that something was not wrong with the hearing utensil on my desk. The Minister said today that this law will make divorce more difficult and slower.
He did not say that.

I know the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Lapointe) has been listening carefully, but I am afraid he will just have to lean over and whisper to his colleague, the Minister of Justice (Mr. MacGuigan), because I made a note of precisely when the Minister made that reference.
As I said, we have two signals coming from this legislation. I think this is one of the difficulties we experience with respect to this legislation. It has been held out to whatever crowd the
Minister and Government spokesmen have been speaking as the basis of great reform, but it depends upon the forum to which they are speaking as to which way they describe that particular reform.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is entirely untrue.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I had to intervene this morning when the Minister was speaking. I would expect the co-operation of all Members on both sides of the House in listening to the very interesting speech of the Hon. Member for Saskatoon West (Mr. Hnatyshyn).

Mr. Speaker, I know when I have hit a responsive chord on the Government side because when I speak the truth with respect to the position the Government has taken, we hear squeals, yelling and whining from the Government benches. It does not affect me at all. I am prepared to set forth on the record what I think are some of the concerns we have regarding this legislation.
At the outset I should remind Hon. Members that 40 per cent of all marriages in this country end in divorce at the present time. In 1982 this translated into some 70,000 divorce decrees being granted. That means 140,000 people were directly affected by the laws relating to divorce.
It must not be forgotten that, in addition to that figure, there are untold thousands of children and relatives who suffered and endured the breakup of marriages. The cost of the people involved cannot be adequately measured. In financial terms the expenditures are enormous. Canadians involved in divorce have spent an estimated $500 million in legal fees alone over the last ten years. Under our present laws, even a straightforward, uncontested petition can result in significant financial hardship for many individuals. In addition, the cost of court administration continues to grow.
Yet in the scheme of things and the way things operate in this area, the financial cost in many cases may not be the most important component of the costs litigants are required to bear. The psychological and emotional costs are more often than not far more significant. Parties to a divorce are put through an emotional wringer in many, many instances. At the time they are dealing with the stress of a family breakup, they must also deal with courts, judges, lawyers and the intricacies of formal divorce proceedings. This process is, when all is said and done, another form of legal proceeding. This means a component common to all legal proceedings, the adversarial component, is still present in the present proposal brought forward by the Minister. It will involve lawyers who are hired and who by and large are involved in pursuing cases on behalf of their clients to ensure that their client receives the best
February 24, 1984

possible result in terms of the relief claimed by the applicant, in terms of the financial settlement and in terms of custody.
Lawyers are used to operating in an adversarial system. I am not criticizing them for that. They do their work. They are trained to pursue their clients' cases in that way, the same as if they would pursue a case on behalf of a commercial client. They are there to get the most they can for their client. They are not, by and large-although there is a tendency to improve the situation-trained in the area of counselling and mediation, which often is so essential in cases of matrimonial breakdown.
Unfortunately, in the process factors that are unique to a divorce proceeding may be ignored and counselling and mediation may be forgotten. As a result, the parties often emerge bitter and mistrustful of their former spouses, lawyers-usually lawyers on the other side-and the judicial system in general. Another consequence is that marriages that may, in fact, be salvaged are not saved because of the adversarial nature of the proceedings in a formal court setting.
In short, I would suggest that anyone who has gone through the process will say that it is very often a most unpleasant one for the participants and often highly traumatic and distressing. Legislation dealing with divorce will necessarily affect hundreds of thousands of Canadians. Such legislation will of necessity deal with a matter of extreme importance to the individuals involved. Therefore the importance of this particular Bill cannot be overstated. Canadians have a right to expect that their elected representatives will give it the care and consideration it deserves.
As I mentioned, the last major changes to the divorce legislation took place some 15 years ago, in 1968. Since that time there have been significant social and economic changes in the structure of Canadian society. New trends have emerged both in judicial approaches to marriage breakdown and in provincial legislation dealing with the division of matrimonial property. During that 15 years numerous groups and agencies have grappled with the problems of divorce and with difficult questions as to just what reforms are desirable.
The Law Reform Commission of Canada studied the matter closely. The Canadian Bar Association and the Law Society of Upper Canada provided detailed recommendations in this area. Changes and reform have been urged by a great many groups and agencies, from church representatives and spokespersons for social workers to a variety and a number of important women's groups. Not all of these parties have called for the same changes; it would have been surprising if they had. However, what is noteworthy is that for a great many years many people have asked for change and reform to our divorce laws. In point of fact, the Minister of Justice has been promising great and sweeping changes for almost as long as he has held his portfolio. When he took over his responsibilities he said that divorce reform was a "top priority". Time and time again the Minister in various fora, in newspapers and in front of the media across the country, promised that new legislation
Divorce Act
would be introduced immediately, if not sooner. Every time I picked up the Monday morning edition of The Globe and Mail there was another article featuring the Minister promising divorce reform and the introduction of sweeping legislation during the course of the coming week. We were repeatedly disappointed until the Minister finally brought forward Bill C-10 as a result of enormous consideration on his part and that of his colleagues.
The fact of the matter is that with all the trumpeting and fanfare preceding the introduction of this Bill, Canadians expected comprehensive, well thought out, effective legislation which would deal with the many problems involved in marriage breakdown and the possibility of salvaging relationships between human beings. We have had reason to expect that, but now I am sorry to report that, as a result of all this cogitation on the part of the Minister and his colleagues, he has come up very much short of what might have been expected on his part.
The Hon. Member for Durham-Northumberland (Mr. Lawrence) has termed the proposal before us as shallow, superficial and simplistic. My colleague was always a Member noted for his understatement of a point of view. When he says that about this particular piece of legislation, I know he knows about which he speaks.
The Minister has addressed himself to the relatively easy question of grounds for divorce. For all intents and purposes he ignored far more difficult and contentious issues, such as maintenance and child custody. In terms of this kind of legislation, unless we deal with these matters the legislation in itself will be wanting and subject to great criticism across the country.
I would like to indicate the depth of concern which has been expressed with respect to this legislation. Many Hon. Members will remember that when the Minister brought down his Bill it was met with the usual approbation by "The Toronto Trudeau Star". It was very much applauded as being a forward-thinking piece of legislation. Even The Toronto Star has now had second thoughts and realizes that the legislation is seriously lacking. In terms of editorial opinion and representations by people who follow the issue and are concerned about it, such as women's groups across the country, they are together and consistent in their criticism of the legislation, not so much because the Minister has tried to do only a few things but because there are many items which should have received attention but received absolutely none.
I could refer to the editorial comments in newspapers across the land, but I would like to quote from the Vancouver Province and its editorial of January 25, which characterized the Bill as "short on courage". A small portion of that editorial reads:
After all the preening and advanced promotion of its divorce law changes, the federal Government has brought forward a mouse ... For six months the Justice Minister ... heralded the proposed changes as his "top legislative priority". The end product is the work of a tired administration sapped of political courage.
That is precisely the point. This Bill does not even come close to dealing adequately with the subject matter. It is a

February 24, 1984
Divorce Act
calculated attempt to give the appearance of action while in fact doing very little at all. It is clear that the Bill requires a great deal of consideration and work to turn it into an acceptable Bill, if it is at all possible. Canadians must be given the opportunity to express their views on such a fundamental topic. It must receive a fair and thorough examination in committee so that we in this Party, as well as Members of the other Parties in the House, can do the job which the Government has apparently abdicated.
I am concerned as well with the legislative initiatives which have been brought forward at this point in time by the Minister and whether we will have sufficient time in the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs to deal in a proper manner with the legislation. He has brought in an omnibus Bill which requires two pages to carry around concerning amendments to the Criminal Code. He has brought in this divorce legislation. His colleague the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) has brought in an important piece of legislation which we are now debating dealing with a civilian security service. A further Bill has been languishing on the Order Paper for some years now. It deals with the grievance procedure in the RCMP. I ask whether or not the Government is serious when it says that it is interested in reform or whether or not this is window dressing with no anticipation of being able to complete our work in committee, even if we worked morning, noon and night to deal with the many topics which the Minister of Justice and the Solicitor General have brought before us for consideration and for ultimate consideration by the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
Much has been made of the fact that if this Bill is passed the traditional grounds for divorce would be eliminated and replaced by the sole ground from this time forward of marriage breakdown. This approach is justified on the basis that fault grounds "encourage the view of divorce as an adversarial conflict between an innocent and guilty spouse". I have already referred to some of the drawbacks in an adversarial system. I have already talked about whether or not the adversarial system is the appropriate one to deal with marriage breakdown.
However, I want to raise with the Minister some of my concerns with respect to the reform that he proposes should be accepted by Parliament. Any lawyer who practises in the field of family law will say that the questions of maintenance, property division and custody of children are the contentious issues in a marriage breakdown. It is on these issues that adversarial conflicts are joined. If there is agreement with respect to these matters, the question of grounds or fault is often of little significance. I suggest that it makes no difference under the present law in my experience.
Although I have not specialized in the practise of family law, members of my law firm who have been involved in it confirm this point. No matter if the grounds are three years, five years, adultery or cruelty, in terms of the dispute that takes place in the court that is often insignificant, if not completely secondary. Where the real dispute takes place is
with respect to the level of maintenance and the whole question of custody.
To be sure, the process of apportioning fault, finding one party guilty of misconduct, may exacerbate the feeling of hurt and embarrassment. However, the elimination of these so-called fault grounds will not necessarily mean the end of the adversarial process. The danger with what the Minister is suggesting is that he may well be throwing the baby out with the bath water. In his attempt to lessen adversarial conflict by eliminating fault grounds, he may well be giving rise to new problems if those grounds are entirely eliminated.
I pose to the Minister that it is not necessarily a question of grounds for divorce being based on fault. Very often they can be regarded as being on the basis of necessity. I want to pursue that and try to examine what might occur in a great number of instances with this proposal which requires a one-year waiting period in all circumstances.
What of the woman who becomes pregnant by a man other than her husband while the marriage is still extant? With the traditional ground of adultery or infidelity gone, the possibility of immediate divorce is eliminated. In fact, if this Bill is passed, the divorce will not be obtained until some time after the child of that liaison is born.
What of the wife who is subject to extreme physical cruelty at the hands of her husband? It may well be that it is in both party's interests, when that circumstance exists, by virtue of the doctrine of necessity, to have an immediate dissolution of the marriage. I ask the Minister this rhetorical question: Must a woman under the circumstances I have indicated be obliged to wait for a rather long period of time, causing great anguish and difficulty?
I want to make another point with respect to the elimination of necessity grounds. In my experience, under the present law judges are often reluctant to make orders for interim relief that may not be made final for an extended period of time. This is based on the knowledge gained by judges that facts that are alleged on interim applications often are in conflict and do not coincide with facts in the final disposition of any matter relating to marriage breakdown or divorce.
Under this Bill, interim relief could and would often extend for a year before such relief could be made final. The Minister will say if there is cruelty that you issue the divorce, and although you cannot get a final decree for a year, you can apply to the judge for a decree of interim alimony. I say to the Minister, because of the experience that I and many lawyers who deal in family law have had, that this may be a great disservice to the party who has every right, because of cruelty or whatever reason, to be living separate and apart from her husband.
The realistic facts are these. In these interim agreements judges have been somewhat reluctant to grant reasonable and adequate interim alimony, even under the present law, pending the completion of the litigation. We should consider these matters in terms of the effect that the sole ground for dissolu-
February 24, 1984

tion may have with respect to people in very difficult circumstances.
The move to eliminate the grounds of necessity requires serious consideration. I understand what the Minister is trying to do with this Bill. By dropping some of the grounds, we may find in the course of our deliberations that it should be sufficient for the parties to have the right to proceed immediately to divorce. We should look at this as the present law may not ameliorate the difficulties that surround the adversarial system.
The second major difficulty with this legislation is in its approach to the whole question of maintenance. This in turn involves the dual question of maintenance criteria and maintenance enforcement. 1 know the Minister spent a long period of time on this matter. I am sure he is sensitive to the very serious criticism that has been put forward regarding the lack of adequate provisions dealing with maintenance enforcement.
In dealing with the issue of maintenance criteria, this Bills sets out a number of objectives that the court should consider in making a maintenance order. While these objectives may well be desirable, what is conspicuously absent from them is any sort of precision. It will be left to the courts to try to establish a systematic method of achieving those enumerated objectives.
The absence of precision, coupled with the clear ambiguity, is objectionable for a number of reasons. First, it is much easier to arrive at a negotiated settlement between lawyers or through mediation if the rights and obligations of the parties involved are precise. The clearer and more explicit the criteria, the fewer things there are to fight about.
If you want a demonstration of this principle, Mr. Speaker, you need only look to provincial laws concerning matrimonial property. In many provinces the law now states that there is a presumption that matrimonial property is to be divided on a fifty-fifty basis. The parties are aware of this, and hence litigation and consequent expenses are significantly reduced. Instead of lawyers' fees eating up the family assets, they now go to the parties involved in the dispute.
A second problem with the stated objectives is that they do not ensure adequate maintenance for one type of situation in particular. I am referring to the common case of a woman who has been married for 20 or 30 years being faced with divorce proceedings. She has devoted her life to her home, husband and family and, as a consequence, the unfortunate fact is that she has few if any marketable skills and little prospect of being in a position to obtain the kind of training to put her back into the workplace so that she can sustain herself or be self-sufficient. Realistically, if her husband petitions for divorce she is not going to be able to support herself.
The Bill presented to us today does not adequately deal with this situation. It is often impractical to suggest that a woman in such circumstances can become economically self-sufficient. Yet even if the court recognizes this, there is no guarantee that the wife will receive maintenance sufficient to live in the manner to which she was accustomed. While her ex-husband
Divorce Act
may still have significant earning potential, the woman may be sentenced to a life of penury and deprivation. Surely it is up to us to direct our minds to seeing if we can structure this legislation to provide as much protection as is possible for women who find themselves in those unfortunate circumstances.
At least as important as the question of how maintenance is determined is the question of how maintenance orders are to be enforced. A maintenance order is of absolutely no use if the maintenance debtor refuses to pay and cannot be forced to pay. It is difficult to say precisely how many maintenance orders are in default at any one time, but estimates indicate that up to 75 per cent of maintenance orders are in default at this time.
This is a shameful and scandalous situation that has been tolerated for far too long in this country. It is too easy for a spouse to evade payment of a court ordered maintenance obligation by simply leaving the jurisdiction. Even if the spouse simply refuses to pay, it leaves an onerous obligation on the other spouse, who is obliged to bring an action to enforce the legitimate order. It invariably results in the administration of justice being brought into disrepute. The spouse, generally speaking the woman, has gone through a harrowing and traumatic divorce proceeding. She has obtained a maintenance order from the court obligating her husband to make payments. Her husband then refuses to pay. How can you explain to that woman that the justice system cannot force her husband to do what the court said he must? You cannot, of course. Meanwhile another person has lost faith in the system which is supposedly in place to protect her and her family.
The other obvious problem with the general unenforceability of maintenance orders is that the Financial burden for family support is lifted from the individual, where it belongs, and transferred to the state, where it does not belong. Surely if the husband has the ability and legal obligation to help support his children, and perhaps his ex-wife, he should be made to do so. The Minister cannot justify his inaction in this area by claiming it is one of provincial responsibility. He has not seen fit to implement the recommendation made by the federal-provincial committee on the enforcement of maintenance and custody orders in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We have.

These recommendations were brought down last year and the Minister has had ample time to consider them. Certainly the proposal put forward by the committee deserves serious consideration.
In addition, they came down clearly in favour of the establishment of a central registry for maintenance and custody orders. The Minister has now said they are giving the most serious and immediate consideration to the final implementation of this concept. However, these are things which should have been pursued with great vigour prior to bringing in this legislation. This should not have come up after the Bill was

February 24, 1984
Divorce Act
introduced in the House. In a planted question on the floor of the House, the Minister was able to stand up and say: "Well, we finally got around to considering this matter and things are looking good. I want to thank my colleague, the Minister responsible for the Status of Women, for all the assistance she has given me".
That, Mr. Speaker, should have been dealt with by any self-respecting Minister of Justice in order to bring it to a conclusion. I believe, and it has now been verified by the Minister himself, that the provincial governments had been prepared to co-operate. He now tells us this is the case. Not before the Bill is brought in, but afterwards, which gives some indication of the bona fides with respect to the amount of time and energy the Minister expended to reach this very important agreement. Even though maintenance enforcement is primarily of provincial concern, surely it is up to the federal Government to show some leadership in resolving the horrendous problems which now exist. Uniform provincial agreements to permit nationwide enforcement of maintenance and custody orders are clearly necessary. No longer should it be possible for a spouse to escape his or her legal obligation simply by pulling up stakes and moving out of the jurisdiction where the original order was made.
When I began my remarks this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, I mentioned the difficulties which can arise when matters end up in the courts and the legal system and lawyers are inserted into the complex factors surrounding marriage breakdown. Unfortunately the legal process often exacerbates many problems rather than diminishes them. A large property or maintenance award may well be obtained at high cost in emotional and psychological terms. Unfortunately it is not possible to completely eliminate this difficulty. However, there are things which can be done to offset the negative aspects of divorce proceedings. In my view this should have been pursued by the Minister and his Government in order to bring some sanity to this whole question.
The Minister will know that we have across this country pilot unified family court projects. These resulted from federal-provincial agreements and involved not only judges with jurisdiction in both the federal and provincial areas of responsibility in these matters, but judges who can hear all these matters as superior court judges. But they also have a very unique capacity which I think is an important ingredient in any so-called reform and our divorce law. That, Mr. Speaker, is the capacity to make available to people faced with this unfortunate circumstance in their marital relationship good pre- and post-divorce counselling services.
I think one of the most successful parts of a unified family court is this unique counselling capacity which exists in the system. I know in my own home city of Saskatoon that we are indeed fortunate to have a unified family court system. I am sure the Minister will agree that these have been very successful enterprises. I think this is the direction in which we as legislators and as Members of Parliament must encourage divorce reform. We can all understand the pre-marriage breakdown counselling. Husband and wife have come in, their
minds are set on dissolution of the marriage, but there is available a service which will bring perspective to the custody of and access to children. It will remove the adversarial atmosphere which exists in the courtroom. From the people I have spoken to who deal in family law, it is amazing the enormously good work which has been done in these counselling services.
This is the kind of expenditure of public funds we on this side of the House would very much encourage the Government to get involved in. It is a meaningful expenditure which, in the final analysis, will save Canadian taxpayers literally millions and millions of dollars lost when one spouse, usually the wife, finds herself on welfare and unable to support herself or her family.
I would also point out, Mr. Speaker, that pre-divorce consultation may in fact have the advantage of allowing people to consider reconciliation in a meaningful way. However, I suggest the post-divorce counselling services are equally important for individuals who have just had their world shattered. The normal situation in a divorce proceeding is that the last we see of these people is when they leave the courtroom hearing with a decree absolute. There is no provision except through welfare departments in some provinces for any kind of counselling in order to assist these single parent families where the change has been very difficult.
When we consider a Bill which will, according to some of the Minister's utterances, facilitate divorce, 1 think we have the responsibility of considering how best to implement counselling and mediation. One way which has worked, as I say, is through the unified family court concept.

speechtext:
