Saskatchewan.

Well, Mr. Speaker, there are examples across this country and I want to bring some to the attention of the Minister. A further example of initiatives in this area can be seen in the approach to mediation and custody disputes in Ontario. The Children's Law Reform Act provides a mechanism whereby a mediator can, at the request of the parties, be appointed. The role of the mediator is to consult with the parties, attempt to reach an agreement between them and ultimately file a full report with the court on the results of the mediation. I think this represents a novel and constructive approach and, along with similar concepts should receive comprehensive review by the committee. I agree with the Minister. Let us look at the experience in Manitoba, in Ontario and in Saskatchewan to see whether we can bring forward proposals that will enhance and improve the legislation.
The long and the short of it is that the Minister promised much and delivered little. We are getting used to that from this Government, of course. Unfortunately, it is the hundreds and thousands of Canadians who will seek divorces in the next
February 24, 1984

few years who will suffer because of the lack of government action.
There are a number of areas that I could deal with but I do not want to spend an inordinate time on this. Many of my colleagues feel strongly about the legislation, feel strongly about support of the family unit and feel strongly about the protection of the rights of people affected by divorce. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald), who is this Party's spokesperson on women's issues, has had a long and distinguished career standing up for the rights of women, particularly the disadvantaged women in our society, those who often have suffered the trauma of divorce. I look forward to her remarks on some of the inconsistencies in this legislative package. She will deal with matters to which I have only had an opportunity to allude in a general way. I look forward to a full and reasonable debate.
There are aspects of the Bill which I think may lead, willy-nilly, to results contrary to those that the Minister intended. For example, we should consider the Minister's idea about trying to take the whole question of divorces arrived at by agreement out of the courts. I understand the motivation of the Minister in this regard.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I regret to interrupt the Hon. Member but his time has expired. He may continue with the unanimous consent of the House. Is it agreed?
Agreed.

I want to conclude with one example, Mr. Speaker. In the present circumstances the law is that even when there are settlements with respect to maintenance and other things that come before a judge in a divorce action, the court is not required to accept that agreement arrived at by the spouses. The idea the Minister put forward would obviate the necessity of a trial where there is consent to divorce proceedings and where all items such as maintenance, dissolution of marriage, custody and other ancillary matters have been settled. It is my experience that in a great number of cases, after observing the litigants first hand and having had an opportunity to examine and cross-examine the parties, the judge will come to the conclusion that such an agreement is not in the best interests of one party or the other. He may feel that the wife is accepting it because she has been harangued and harassed and would be in a difficult position if she did not accept the husband's offer. In those circumstances, whether the parties like it or not, the judge may not accept the agreement and rule that the maintenance be twice as much, for example, and if the wife does not want to pursue it, then so be it.
These are the things that I think we must examine. We must examine the Bill and determine whether it is constructive and thorough and if it will bring about appropriate reform. The Minister has taken a one dimensional approach, I think, but we need an approach that is consistent with the welfare of the men and women concerned, that is consistent with the welfare
Divorce Act
of the children of those marriages and consistent with the principles of equity and fairness regarding maintenance orders and the enforcement of them.
I can assure the Minister that on this side of the House we regard this as a very important piece of legislation and he will receive a number of constructive suggestions from my colleagues.
I want to thank Hon. Members for their indulgence in allowing me extra time to speak, Mr. Speaker. I also want to tell the Minister that because we find the Bill lacking in so many essential elements in its present form, we in this Party are unable to support it.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to take part in this extremely important debate on divorce. This is the first reform in our divorce legislation in Canada since 1968. There are roughly 60,000 divorces in the country every year, half of them involving minor children. It has been estimated that up to 40 per cent of first marriages presently undertaken will end in divorce, so it is a matter that touches a large number of people.
Reform is needed, Mr. Speaker, and the Bill will accomplish one major reform. It also deals with a few minor reforms. However, it is grossly deficient in a number of other matters, especially in the area of maintenance. I shall deal with these deficiencies at some length.
Let me begin with the area in which there is broad agreement, that of marriage breakdown as the sole grounds for divorce. It has been said that divorce does not cause marriage breakdown; unsatisfactory marriages do. A decree of divorce does not kill a marriage; it certifies that it is dead. This is the spirit behind the approach to marriage breakdown as the sole grounds for divorce. It is a principle that the New Democratic Party has accepted for many years. It has been on our books since 1967, and a large number of women's organizations have recommended recognition of this principle as the sole grounds for divorce. There is overwhelming support for it among women's groups. Let me quote from a couple of them, Mr. Speaker.
The Catholic Women's League, an important women's organization in Canada, in its brief to the Minister of Justice (Mr. MacGuigan) said that the present system of having to air one's marital laundry in a public court room seems both demeaning and time consuming. It is obvious that at a time when the matter is being heard by a divorce court judge, any possibility of reconciliation has long since dissipated. The organization says that the present system appears to lend itself to a good deal of mutual disrespect and disposes of any possible future friendship the spouses may have. Furthermore, it believes that the accusations and counter-accusations of the present adversarial system seem to do a great deal of harm to the familial relationship which oftentimes must survive the dissolution of a marriage because of children.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, it is especially because of the children that we are concerned to see marriage breakdown established as the sole grounds for divorce. Having it so

February 24, 1984
Divorce Act
established will make it easier for arrangements for custody and maintenance to be facilitated.
The National Association of Women and the Law says that to attempt to focus upon a single marital fault on the part of one of the spouses as the cause of the breakdown of marriage is most often a distortion of the marriage relationship. It says that hostility between the spouses on the issue of grounds must necessarily taint negotiations between the parties on corollary issues where important decisions must be made on more relevant considerations such as the best interests of the children.
The one-year waiting period to establish marriage breakdown, of course, is more controversial. Some people think it is too short and some think it is too long. Some women's organizations have suggested that there ought to be no fixed waiting period at all. The National Association of Women and the Law and the National Action Committee on the status of women have taken this position, and they have reasons for doing so. Let me quote the National Action Committee. It says:
Marriage must be recognized as an equal partnership, entered into voluntarily by a woman and a man. Once one of the parties has decided that the partnership is not working, the relationship is clearly ended and no legal rule will make it work. The spouses should be able to declare that the marriage has broken down, and that declaration should be regarded as sufficient to prove the breakdown. Proof of separation or fault should not be required.
This is quite an extreme statement and lots of people would disagree with it. Clearly, the one-year period to establish marriage breakdown is a compromise between those who think it is too long and those who think it is too short. I suspect that there would never be a period on which we could agree as being ideal for all situations.
I consulted a number of ministers and priests in my own riding. We had an excellent discussion on this subject. Some felt that one year was too short. Some felt that there might be greater reconciliation achieved if there were a longer period. None of them, however, felt it was easy to arrive at a time, and there were no great objections to the period of one year. The one year seems at least not unreasonable.
With respect to support for the family, some groups, particularly the Catholic bishops, have argued that instead of making divorce easier, we should be making marriage more difficult. It is indeed true that it is easier to get a marriage licence than to get a driver's licence. Certainly, I myself and the New Democratic Party have vigorously supported all kinds of measures to assist the family; family allowance, maternity benefits, parental leave and daycare provisions. I welcome as well the provision in this legislation which would promote reconciliation within the marriage itself. However, I have to remind people who would like to see marriage made more difficult that marriage itself comes under provincial jurisdiction. It is not possible in the course of amending the Divorce Act to deal directly with that question. We, of course, do have responsibilities as parliamentarians to support the family with many other provisions.
With respect to custody arrangements, here again we do see some improvements, and I welcome them. It will be clearly stated in the legislation that the best interests of the child will be the principal factor in determining custody. There are provisions for awards of joint custody and for persons other than the parents to have custody, possibly the grandparents, and access could be established for the grandparents in a court order. This is certainly an important reform. There is also provision for independent representation of the children in court.
I feel that the Bill could be more explicit in establishing the criteria by which the best interests of the children would be determined by a court. The Law Reform Commission of Canada made some recommendations back in 1975, and these have been taken up by Ontario, and, indeed, used more widely in Canada. I will cite some of them; the emotional tie of the child to the persons claiming custody, the preferences of the child, the length of time the child has had with the person claiming custody, plans for the upbringing of the child, the capacity of the parents for guidance, education and providing the necessities of life, any special needs of the child, the stability of the custodial household, and the relationship to the child, whether by blood, adoption or any other kind. We do, therefore, have some criteria and perhaps it should be in the legislation. Other lists could be provided, and the National Association of Women and the Law, I believe, has a very good list as well. It refers to the mental, emotional and physical needs of the child and the ability of each spouse to provide for such needs. There is the effect of disruption on the child's sense of continuity and need for stability, the views and preferences of the child where such can be reasonably ascertained, the need to foster access to the non-custodial spouse, and the relationship among other children in the family. I believe some greater specificity on the criteria would be important to have in the legislation.

Even though we agree with the principle of marriage breakdown being the only ground for divorce, we of the New Democratic Party do not support this Bill on second reading. The drawbacks of this Bill are much too serious and, if it is adopted, it will have dire consequences, especially for women and children who are economically dependent. Although current alimony payments are already inadequate, the proposed amendments, will make the situation of dependent women and children even worse than it is today. The trend nowadays seems to be towards lower alimony payments over ever shorter periods of time. Yet this Bill goes further in the sense that it advocates fixed periods of time and even less generous alimony payments. Why? Apparently because this Bill considers economic independence as something which is due. Indeed it is a reasonable objective, particularly in the case of young childless couples where both spouses are still working. I am reading the text of the Department of Justice on divorce.
It may be true that in many instances the dependent spouse ought to be entitled to long-term financial support, but that is
February 24, 1984

not always the case. After leaving the labour market in order to run the household and take care of the children, the dependent spouse may find it difficult, if not altogether impossible, to earn a decent income after the divorce. This decrease in one's ability to earn a living is a direct consequence of marriage and should be taken into account when figuring out the amount of financial support. In many cases, however, the dependent spouse might be able to return to the labour market, particularly if measures are taken to enable him or her to get vocational training or go back to school. Some day, that spouse might become self-supporting and financially independent.
The Department is aware that it may be impossible for some women to become economically independent, according to this Bill, yet the Bill does imply that all women are financially independent. Quite simply, the Bill fails to take into account the real situation of a great many women who have looked after the household and raised their children on a full-time basis over a number of years.
Let us admit that there is indeed economic dependence in such a case. Take for instance a women aged 55 who has not had a paid job for 30 or 35 years. She quit working when her first child was born. Her work at home has made it possible for her husband to take the technical training needed to pursue his own career. At the age of 55, that woman cannot make up for lost time. Without any experience on the labour market, what can she do? She could earn a living washing dishes in a restaurant, but is that fair? Let us suppose that this woman had been the wife of a doctor, a lawyer or a Member of Parliament. Is it reasonable for her standard of living to go down that much? Are the highly abstract principles of economic independance, justice and maintenance of a comparable standard of living without significance for the lawyers at the Department of Justice? Unfortunately, the Bill is firm in this regard. The only criterion applicable to maintenance payments is avoidance of serious economic conditions. Maintenance payments will no longer promote economic independence and avoid hardship. That is all! According to the criteria proposed in this Bill, I would say that the principle of economic independence for every man and woman should be outweighed by the concept of justice.
There are various types of marriage. Especially where marriages having lasted a long time are concerned, other criteria should be developed. The other basic deficiency I find in this Bill is the absolute lack of practical provisions for the collection of maintenance payments. As we know, unfortunately, most maintenance payments ordered by the courts are never made. About 75 per cent of maintenance payments are in arrears with the result that thousands of women and children are living in proverty without adequate means of support. These figures are well-known and cannot be questioned. In addition, many practical solutions have been suggested to change the alimony system. During the summer of 1983, a federal-provincial task force came up with recommendations
Divorce Act
for the reform of the present system. Yet, this Bill contains no practical answers.
A reform of our divorce legislation is not acceptable without a reform of the provisions to enforce maintenance orders.
We have heard too much talk about this Bill legislating no fault divorce. The fact is that really it legislates no responsibility divorce. The provisions for maintenance in Bill C-10 are unrealistic, short-sighted, unfair and will cause real harm to women predominantly, and in some cases to children, if it is passed.
In the rarified atmosphere of the Ministry of Justice the pursuit of an abstract principle, that of economic independence, is considered more important than dealing with the real problems we all know too much about. The goal of economic independence is suitable for many divorced people. The paper outlining the Bill admits it is not realistic for all. It is what is in the Act that counts rather than what is in the discussion paper when it comes to a case in court.
Many women's groups and expert individuals have made very good and persuasive arguments for different provisions. I would like to quote Judge Rosalee Abella from a paper entitled "Economic Adjustment on Marriage Breakdown". Judge Abella notes that spousal independence should not be taken too literally. "Independence will not be possible for every one". It should not be used, as it has been, prematurely, and certainly not where the realities of the marketplace and community make it impractical. If the wife is at home, it is usually because both spouses expect it and often want her there. To suggest to these women that they should become independent when their marriages dissolve is to ignore the economics of their situations. Though they are legally considered equal partners in their former marriage, because of the marriage and because of community expectations, they undertook a role which, though it created equal status, did not create equal access to independent sources of income.
According to Judge Abella, maintenance should not be paid because the wife was formerly her husband's dependant but because she was and is his equal partner who has needs which the partnership created and encouraged. Ideally these payments should be at a level to permit both of them to continue at the same standard of living they had in the marriage.
The years when the husband was increasing his educational and career prospects were years which increasingly diminished the wife's prospects in the labour force. It is the traditional marriage partnership itself over the years which creates an economic disability. The economics of indefinite support flows naturally from the economics of most current marriage relationships.
The National Action Committee on the status of women has made its recommendations on maintenance very clear. They are more realistic and fairer than the ones in the Bill before us today. The National Action Committee suggests that we con-

February 24, 1984
Divorce Act
sider three different types of marriage. For some the principle of economic dependence simply as it is is quite adequate. These are younger couples who split up without either partner having been harmed in the sense of an economic dependence being created in the course of the marriage. When a spouse's capacity to support herself or himself has been reduced by the division of tasks within the family, temporary support should be granted to allow that spouse to continue to be a full-time parent and allow time to upgrade skills and re-enter the labour market. This should include general education up to and including university.
Let us look at the situation of a long-term homemaker where a permanent dependency has been created. In divorces following marriages of long duration where one spouse was a homemaker and a permanent dependency was created, longterm maintenance should be ordered and the criteria used should be fairness and justice. Such wholly dependent spouses should not be expected to seek employment in occupations far below their previous living standards. For example, a homemaker married to a doctor for 30 years should not be denied long-term support for the reason that she could support herself if she found a job as a sales clerk or cleaning lady.
The National Association of Women and the Law has offered a set of similar criteria beginning with a mutual obligation to take all reasonable steps to become financially independent, but conceding that where this is not possible because of the duties undertaken in the marriage, long-term maintenance is required.
Most maintenance payments ordered by the courts are not made. It is true that to improve collection much must be done at the provincial level and some changes require joint action of the federal and provincial Governments. Many measures could and should be taken under federal jurisdiction. One of the main contributions the federal Government could make is in the location of persons defaulting on court ordered maintenance payments. If a defaulter leaves the province to avoid payment, he may be receiving unemployment insurance or paying his income tax and there are records by which his new address could be located. There is a concern for privacy, but I would suggest this does not outweigh the concern that children be supported and dependent spouses receive justice. All federal records, save the census, should be open for the location of addresses of defaulters in the case of court ordered maintenance.
Legislation is needed to provide such access and should be dealt with, if not in the same legislation, in companion legislation at the same time. Given the complacency of the Ministry of Justice, I am not optimistic that we can wait for it to deal with this matter. The recommendations of the Law Reform Commission of Canada on this subject go back to 1976. The Royal Commission on the Status of Women in Canada reported on the deficiencies in 1970. It has had a long time to work out practical criteria with the provinces.
Consistent with the proposal for improving access to addresses to locate the defaulters is the notion of interception. Wages and salaries are subject to garnishment for non-payment. I suggest the same principle should hold for other moneys under federal jurisdiction. Income tax refunds, unemployment insurance, interest on Canada saving bonds, and pensions are all moneys under federal jurisdiction. Why should they be exempt? In the time of the marriage itself these moneys would be shared for the support of the whole family. After a divorce why should they become the private property of only the breadwinner, while other members of the family suffer want as a result? It is time the federal Government stopped blaming the provinces for inaction and did what it can under its own jurisdiction.
Good divorce law should take into account pensions. After all, pensions are deferred wages and salaries. When a couple divide their labours so that one joins the work force and earns an income and the other stays home to look after the home and raise the children, there is an implied contract that that income is for the support of all of them. The same should hold for pensions which are simply a carry-over of that income. Pension splitting is only fair, but Bill C-10 does not deal with it.
In the Budget reference is made to the Government's intention to split Canada Pension Plan credits on marriage breakdown. Certainly the Government is recognizing the principle and the Minister referred to it earlier today saying it would be done for other pensions under federal jurisdiction. I remind Hon. Members that this was not said in the Budget and we have not seen the legislation. Given the slowness of action on the part of the Government and the complacency on this subject, I would not be optimistic. 1 would like to see all pensions under federal jurisdiction dealt with promptly. That would include pensions of MPs, Senators, judges and federal public servants.
Last year the Judges Act was amended but this was not dealt with. It could have been dealt with then. After all, judges are making decisions about the livelihood of dependent members in families. Their own pensions do not permit credit splitting. Judges should have model provisions for pensions if they are going to be enforcing the law for other people.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I would like to refer to the issue of unified family courts. This is a very important reform. Lawyers, social workers, women's organizations and so forth have recommended the institution of unified family courts on a comprehensive basis. Experiments have been made and it has been found that they are better. They provide counselling services, they are less expensive for access and for changing maintenance orders. There are many conveniences in having unified family courts. It is difficult for people to go from court to court, from superior court to provincial courts and to family courts. This is a reform which must be dealt with. 1 am just not satisfied that the recommendations on it are being considered. There should be legislation on it. It should be possible for any province that wishes to establish a unified family court to do so.
February 24, 1984

To conclude, I say that Bill C-10, is grossly deficient. It must go back to the drawing board. I do not accept the Minister's excuse that we cannot do more in the present context. The Minister himself is an expert in omnibus Bills. We had a 306 page Bill on criminal law legislation. Surely this is an area on which there should be an omnibus Bill. It should be omnibus on divorce, to deal with all the related issues such as the enforcement of maintenance payments, the establishment of unified family courts, credit splitting of pensions by judges, and income tax access and statistical record access for the location of defaulters. These are all federal statutes which need quite modest amendments. However, the principle is important. When this does not take place people really do suffer.
If the Department cannot draft suitable legislation, it ought to hire someone who can. I suggest that the Minister withdraw the Bill and bring it back with suitable amendments. We do not need more study because we know what needs to be done. I can assure the Minister of my Party's support for speedy passage when he brings back a Bill that really deals with the issues of maintenance, a Bill which is fair and deals with the issue adequately and concretely.

Mr. Speaker, I know the Hon. Member is seeking to ask questions but questions are not permitted with the first three speakers. Questions may be permitted with the round I am starting. We will welcome the intervention of the Hon. Member from Hamilton at that time.
When I look at this Bill, I call it swinging door legislation. Marriage in Canada is destined to become a swinging door affair. It is extraordinarily easy to get married, notwithstanding the rather strict requirements of many established churches for people to attend marriage preparation courses. While many people take those courses, and I am pleased that they do, they in themselves are no guarantee that a marriage may not break down. A mere trip to a justice of the peace, the deputy registrar of vital statistics in any city or some "marrying Sam" is evidence enough that if certain people perhaps have an amorous or physical desire for one another they can satisfy themselves under the cover of legality. But surely a marriage based upon that alone will not last.
What I and, I am sure, many Hon. Members and hundreds of thousands of Canadians are concerned about is that this Bill is frankly an attack on the family and its continued existence. Marriage should not be buried as a traditional way of life that has gone out of style. That is not the purpose of marriage.
The purpose of marriage is essentially the procreation and raising of children by a man and a woman. Through the years it is married people who have produced and raised children. Are we now to make a sort of rabbit colony relationship in which man meets woman, man likes woman, woman likes man, bingo, they live together and produce children? Is that going to be our concept of life?
Divorce Act
I suggest to the House that this Bill is in many ways part of this, shall we say "easy does it" mentality of the 1960s and 1970s that has permeated through to certain academic levels, certain levels among social workers, among the so-called intelligentsia and sophisticates. The mentality is that if a couple of people get tired of one another or if a particular way of life is not satisfactory, the man need only go out and shuck his wife as he would discard his suit or the wife may discard her husband as she would her year-old dress. This Bill merely reflects that attitude. I do not know that Canadian society will improve as a result thereof.
This Bill has encountered a good deal of opposition. One might expect the Conference of Catholic Bishops to have their say, and to their credit they have done so. It is an area in which they have a right and obligation to speak. There are other church groups and organizations which must look after the children of many of this mismatings and casual matings that we have in modern day society. They also have to look after wives who are discarded.
Incidentally, this divorce law is in many ways no different from some of our veterans affairs legislation. That legislation allows a veteran, under the insurance plan, merely to put aside his wife and live notoriously in the open with another woman. After a year, if he is not in a position to get remarried, he can merely designate his female companion as a beneficiary under the policy. There are other similar features about common law living with regard to veterans' pensions. It is "easy does it."
We must reflect upon whether Canadian society has become a rabbit hutch society. Many of my colleagues have criticized the philosophy behind this legislation. May I say that I have before me a Department of Justice hand-out of information which is printed in the National Review that is published by the Canadian Bar Association. The only thing I can say about the Department of Justice publicist who wrote this is that I wish he had learned his English. We are at repeated points. Just to take one, the word "alternatives" is used to describe numerous options. Let that individual go back and find out what the word "alternative" means. It means one of two, not one of many. There is a column replete with the misuse of that word. That is not good enough for the Department of Justice. We are faced here according to this learned person, with a span of 15 years from the last divorce amendments and consequently there must now be a change in the Divorce Act to comply with social developments. What utter piffle!
We remember before when the Divorce Act was changed when cruelty, desertion for three years, adultery, and several other sex-related crimes were the sole grounds of divorce. Of course, that really did set up, at times, an adversarial form of dealing with divorce, an accusation of adultery perhaps when quite often there was not that situation. There was the business of spurious grounds for divorce in manufactured cases, the old motel room routine; what we used to see so often before the Private Members' Committee of the Senate on Divorce. There was a whole industry in the Province of Quebec, which did not

February 24, 1984
Divorce Act
on any grounds allow for divorce. We had this sort of set up divorce machinery. Yet the statistics referred to in this Department of Justice release show that only one in 20 divorces may be contested. Usually divorce is not contested on the grounds of whether there was cruelty or whether there were grounds for divorce. The divorce is contested as a result of a refusal to agree or an inability to agree on the separation of assets, or on the size of the monthly maintenance for the spouse and, if there are children, for the children. That is the nub of why there are contests.
Then, I regret to say, there are some cases that finish up before the court because of the crass ignorance and incompetence of counsel who are advising the parties concerned. I am ashamed sometimes to see the performances of some of my fellow barristers, particularly in matters of this kind. There was always the fee hunter who did not care about what he had to do under the Act but wanted to finish up in court because he could then collect more in fees. Not only ambulance chasers do you find among the legal profession, but divorce hounds. That has its influence on that one person in 20. 1 would go as far as to say that possibly one in 30 divorces is contested. Is that sufficient reason, one in 30, to get into this open door of no fault? After one year of the filing of a petition for no fault divorce, the decree may be granted. But, Mr. Speaker, there are 90 days of cohabitation allowed, either continuously or cumulatively, after that one year following the filing of the petition. What is this filing for petition for divorce with weekend rights, visation and cohabitation? That is really a fine way of doing it, is it not? I will admit that it might be hard to penalize a person who has made a serious effort at reconciliation who has lived with his or her spouse during that period of attempted reconciliation for two or three months and then finds it is absolutely impossible to reconcile. Therefore, that person is excused. But I know how it is going to work out in the courts, the same way as it was 15 years ago when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), as Minister of Justice, brought forward the changes in the Divorce Act. That was supposed to provide for marriage counselling and an attempt at reconciliation. I know for a fact that that was the biggest hoax ever perpetrated on Canadians. Divorce lawyers did not even pretend to refer anyone to a family counselling agency. There was mere lip service paid to that provision. That is why I say this Bill pays the same lip service to reconciliation and to efforts to preserve the marriage. That is why I am against this Bill.
If marriage is worth something, it is worth people putting something into it to make it work. That includes going to marriage consellors, proper marriage counsellors, not some social divorce lawyer who may take off his coat and say, "I am a marriage counsellor now," to make the marriage work possibly after a serious spat.
I invite Hon. Members or anyone who reads or who hears what I have had to say to look into their own family to see how many young couples have separated over a stupid little quarrel where each one took the high ground and gathered around himself or herself people who said, "Yes, you are doing the right thing." They may be people who were possibly unprepared for marriage. But there are people who fall into the hands of right-meaning relatives, clergy, counsellors or family service bureaux. If people really mean anything to one another they will make a sincere effort to see if they can find a way to patch up their differences. Sometimes it takes an extra step or an extra mile to achieve success. Apparently that is not the rule today. It is too much effort to patch it up and it is too easy to get a divorce. They feel, what is the difference; they can be married to someone else within six months. Maybe the girl the chap has married is not as glamorous over the breakfast table as she was at some dinner or at some dance; maybe he has halitosis in the morning or he is grumpy. Well, if all those things cannot be cured by some good will and change on the part of both parties, both of them are pretty poor stuff to start with.
I say that this Bill is deficient in that it makes insufficient provision for appropriate counselling and efforts at reconciliation to preserve the marriage. What should be the objective of any matrimonial legislation? It should not be to split the parties but to preserve them, if at all possible. I have seen some actions involving serious marriage offences. As a matter of fact I could cite two examples of young couples who were married in September and obtained their decree absolute the following March.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make one or two observations which coincide very much with what the Hon. Member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) has just enunciated. Personally I would like to see very few divorce actions, but the reality of today is such that this is not possible. Divorce actions really penalize a third party, the children, and are certainly the basis of a great deal of misbehaviour and insecurity on the part of children and further breakdown of families. However, I want to expand somewhat on the aspect of divorce about which the Hon. Member for Edmonton West spoke so eloquently, that is, the responsibility of the legal profession in assessing whether or not proper counselling or support has been given to the couple considering divorce.
As I understand it, every lawyer is expected to sign a warrant to the effect that every conceivable approach has been taken in order to keep the marriage together. This may vary from province to province, yet when one hears the duration between the time an action is started and divorce is granted, it
February 24, 1984

appears that this has not been carried out. Among the people I have seen in the practice of medicine, there has been very little attempt made to bring these couples together. This is a reflection of negligence on the part of the legal profession. In the medical profession, the greater the challenge, the harder the research work and the harder the practitioner works to find a solution to the problem. In the legal profession the common practice has been to go through with divorce actions as rapidly as possible and not give the needed social support to the couples.
A second aspect which is of concern to me is again the one year duration in the Bill. A divorce action is a very serious emotional experience for both men and women. Much reference has been made to women, but I would like to indicate that men go through the same emotionally disturbed period. There are many who require as much as a year to think rationally and to plan their lives as they had originally intended. Some steps must and should be taken to assess whether or not these people were able to assimilate intelligently the counselling and support given in order to keep a marriage together.
I agree with the Hon. Member for Edmonton West that very often the obstacle or barrier to bringing a couple together is minimal and with expert support could be remedied. On that account I feel that one year is too short a period of time to bring about corrective, remedial action. I feel that that period of time should be reconsidered.
I just wanted to bring those two observations to the attention of the House in the hope that they will be considered further in the deliberation of this Bill.

Mr. Speaker, unlike most of those who rise to speak on Bills and say that they are delighted to have the opportunity, I do not intend to make any such statement at the beginning of my comments. I am anything but delighted to speak on this Bill or enter into debate on it. 1 am definitely and deeply displeased to have to speak in this debate because I feel that the Bill is a shoddy piece of work, brought before the House immaturely, and is really a disservice to the House in its present form. It is ill-considered, to put it at its mildest, and it is a disgrace as law and an insult to the institution of marriage.
However, I am on my feet and I intend to indicate my views on this Bill. First, I think it is odd. Perhaps odd is not the correct word. There may be another word which will generate itself as I continue. However, there are three Bills now before us which are intended to go through the House on second reading and be referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. I cannot really make out whether it is honestly intended by the Government that these three Bills should become law or whether they are just being put forward as a token of the intention of the Government to do something about the three matters.
One subject is of course the security intelligence Bill which has been before the House but second reading of which has not been concluded. The second one is this divorce Bill, which I
Constitution Act, 1867
say is a disgrace to the House and is offensive in the manner in which it has been put forward and the manner in which it covers the purported matter of the Bill. The third one is that very thick Bill, the Criminal Code amendments, which again offends every good legislative taste. I am not sure whether the intention is that these three Bills be passed by the House or whether it is just a device.
If I may call it four o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I will continue at the next opportunity.

subtopic: CONSTITUTION ACT, 1867 REQUEST TO CHANGE BOUNDARIES OF NATIONAL CAPITAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think we have a rather unusual and even bizarre situation here this afternoon. About two or three years ago, we debated a proposal tabled by the Hon. Member for Hull (Mr. Isabelle) on-I am not sure it was the same subject-the amalgamation or twinning of Hull with Ottawa, to make them both the capital of this country. Or maybe it was to create a National Capital Region that would include Hull. In any case, it concerned the City of Hull and area. However, this time, something funny is going on with the period set aside for Private Members' Business. We start with a first draw for fifty, more or less. Then, when it is a Member's turn to present a Bill or a motion or some Private Bill, he has the right to do

February 24, 1984
Constitution Act, 1867
so. However, I see that on January 20, Bill C-206 was debated for one hour. The Hon. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, actually, I know what the Hon. Member is attempting to do ... Listen, I have much sympathy for what he is attempting to do.
Legally, the National Capital is encompassed within the very narrow limits of the City of Ottawa. I suggest there are as many people, if no more, who live in what they consider as Greater Ottawa, an area we think of as the National Capital! I know that my colleague from Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton (Mr. Dick), and also the two Hon. Members who spoke before favour the idea. Yes! That may make sense! But it must be remembered that, just because Air Canada mentions Ottawa-Hull in its schedules, that does not mean that Ottawa-Hull is the National Capital. No more than Toronto-Hamilton, which appear as twin cities in the same schedule are one city. They
February 24, 1984

are neighbour cities, but not part of the same urban centre. There are many such examples.
I can see some constitutional problems. Naturally, some of you will remind me that there should be consultation with the provinces about the site of the Capital. I know that there is a National Capital Region unilaterally declared by the federal Government and which includes some areas in Quebec, like the entire Gatineau Park, but no agreement has been reached on that point, at least I do not know of any. The Hon. Member suggests that a legal authority exists and that we would merely need an order in council to determine the area included in the Capital. It would be the National Capital Region including appropriate towns and suburbs. I am not quite so sure. It seems to me that it could give rise to a confrontation, especially with the Quebec government. I think that it would almost be like a declaration of war. The province of Ontario could very well say: the provinces are entitled to establish towns within their limits and if necessary to alter the limits of cities or municipalities under such or such an administrative procedure. Well, what can you expect? And we have seen municipalities on the other side of the Ottawa River being merged and made into one city through by-laws under the authority of the Government of Quebec. We all know that. But now, however, we are talking about an order in council issued by the federal Cabinet and stating that henceforth the City of Hull will be part of Canada's capital. Hull would be in the National Capital. What would be the legal consequences? I read the speech of the Hon. Member, but I did not find any reference to the legal consequences of such action. Of course, he did mention certain advantages which would flow from that and would affect the region of Hull as well as Ottawa, but we have not heard anything about some of the negative consequences and it seems to me that we are entitled to a word of explanation before we even consider adopting this Bill, or any other on the same subject, and sending it to Committee. It is not after adopting the Bill that we should have explanations which might perhaps make us change our mind and decide to withdraw our support. You know, Mr. Speaker, we have a practice here whereby, if a Bill is passed on second reading, the principle of the Bill is adopted. I for one do not see it that way and I say that it is wrong because Bill C-206 appears on the Order Paper for second reading and reference to such or such Committee of the House where the Bill would be considered and then reported. It might be reported with an amendment which would have been approved by the majority on the Committee and which might or right not be accepted by the House. An amendment could very well be tabled and debated in this House and the Bill could then be read for the second time. This is the way it goes. The report of the committee of the whole is then agreed upon and the Chair says: "The Bill is read for the second time." We are now being told that, after going through this stage in committee of the whole and after the Bill has been voted on at second reading, it has definitely been accepted or approved in principle. That is false, complete-
Constitution Act, 1867
ly false, but the truth has to be pointed out to these people, beginning with the Prime Minister, because he is always saying that once you have agreed to a Bill you are marked forever, which is completely false, because the Bill is accepted in principle only after its referral here, to the committee, and after the Chair has called the vote at the second reading stage. The same is true, Mr. Speaker, with the procedure in this case. Committee chairmen who do not accept that you put forward amendments because the principle of the Bill has been adopted and the amendment flies in the face of that principle. So this cannot be, you did not present it a second time for acceptance.
I would appreciate that, as a conclusion to this debate, the hon. member speak of certain legal implications he anticipates, and also indicate his view as to the attitude of the Province of Quebec and the Province of Ontario, which are the provinces affected. Frankly, I would have this to say, Mr. Speaker, in conclusion. Do you know that the people in Edmonton would have something to say on the composition of the national capital? It belongs to them and to me, a resident, a property owner in the City of Ottawa, as much as to the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Isabelle).
Hon. Members opposite also, and the citizens of their towns have a voice as to what should happen to the National Capital.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I decided to say a few words about the Bill presented by the Hon. Member for Hull (Mr. Isabelle) because having observed his attempts over the last few years to accomplish this change I can see that even now there is some disagreement or lack of understanding of what he is trying to do. Basically he is simply trying to amend Section 16 of the Constitution Act of 1867; in other words to have the national capital of Canada designated the national capital area.
Over the last few years the Hon. Member for Hull has tried to convince Parliament that since 1858 things have changed drastically and so other things should change as well. One of the changes is introduced in the Bill. On numerous occasions he has pointed out that Parliament has expanded to the Quebec side, that the National Capital Region includes municipalities in Ontario and Quebec. He therefore asks the question, why not make it the capital of Canada? Ottawa and Hull and the surrounding areas equal the National Capital Region.
If we look at the remarks made by the Hon. Member for Hull when introducing the Bill, we will see that on January 20, as reported at page 617, he said:
-if we refer to the history of the national capital area, we see that since the small village of Bytown was selected by the Queen in 1858, it was then ridiculed and called a forest centre and a capital of logs, the City of Ottawa as such has constantly developed.
The reason why I am asking for that amendment is that since the time of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, Sir Robert Borden and even the Right Hon. Mackenzie King, we have always wanted to make of the capital of Canada a national symbol, the seat of our national languages or, if you prefer, the beating heart of our nation.

February 24, 1984
Constitution Act, 1867
Up to now, I think that we have always thought of the capital of Canada as a city in Ontario. I have nothing against Ontario or Ottawa, but throughout the years, we have asked the Federal Government to contribute to the beautification of the region and we have been saying that it should not be restricted to the city of Ottawa. Parliament has continued to expand the region on the Quebec side, in the Outaouais region, and we are now saying that the National Capital Region is a product of Canadian federalism and reflects many of the familiar political, social, linguistic and cultural differences and ambiguities of Canadian society. It is typical of Canada.
In other words, it is a simple matter. The National Capital Region should be the capital of Canada. The Hon. Member for Hull has referred to the positive results of such change over the years. One of the things he has always concentrated on is that it would lead to increased co-operation not, as the former speaker said, to problems. What the Hon. Member for Hull is saying is that it would lead to increased co-operation between the municipalities. He explained that in his last speech when he said:
Whenever we have asked for the co-operation of the various regional governments, it has always been a difficult proposition. This is why over the years I have always advocated a federal district, in order that the federal Government be at home here. But this is not for tomorrow, because we know what came out of the so-called co-operation between the various levels of government, both local and provincial.
The Hon. Member for Hull represents his constituents as well as or better than most Members in the House. He made a statement in introducing his Bill which I thought was interesting. I believe his comments were to the effect that because of the present situation on both sides of the river, it is the most over-governed and overtaxed region of Canada. Why is that, Mr. Speaker? The Hon. Member for Hull says it is because of this complete lack of co-operation between the various levels of government, local and provincial.
In reviewing the objections to the Hon. Member's proposition over the years, a couple of things stand out. It has been said that it is not a simple matter to do this; it is very, very complicated; it is difficult to amend Section 16. I should like to refer the House to what the Hon. Member has said repeatedly over the years. It is reported at page 618 of Hansard as follows:
To those who suggest that an extraordinary process is required for amending Section 16, I say all that is needed is an Order in Council, simply adding Hull and the surrounding municipalities on both sides of the river, so that Canada's National Capital truly reflects the daily life of every Canadian. Because certainly visitors, whether they come from British Columbia or from New Brunswick or Prince Edward Island, are not particularly enthralled when coming to Ottawa to visit just another Ontario City.
When the Hon. Member presented his Bill, some politicians provincially and some federally accused him of trying to "get rid" of Ottawa. In all the statements the Hon. Member has made he has clarified this matter. I should like to quote briefly from his speech of January 20, 1984 in the Chamber when he said, as reported in Hansard at the botton of page 618:
-we should make Ottawa part of the National Capital Region just as all the other municipalities which are now part of the National Capital Region. And I am sure that members of the House are aware of this major problem of a capital for a young country such as Canada, for we have had a flag for some twenty years and we have a practically new, at least freshly patriated Constitution. In my opinion, what really matters now is to endow ourselves with a capital which clearly reflects the wills, aspirations and modus vivendi of all Canadians.
At that stage, Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member got to the exact point of his campaign over the years with this Bill. He went on to say:
It should occupy a neutral ground, outside the territory of any individual province-
The Hon. Member for Hull (Mr. Isabelle) continued:
-I just cannot understand how a province such as Ontario can logically have two capitals. If there is disunity, if the West feels alienated, it may be because we have no meeting point where we could all get together and feel at home as Canadians. People from western Canada think that they are away visiting eastern Canada when they come to this Ontario city, and those from eastern Canada think they have gone West when they are in the same Ontario city.
How true that is, Mr. Speaker. The Hon. Member for Hull went on to say:
Therefore, to dispel any doubt and give Canada a new image or impetus, in line with the novelties we have known over the past few years, including the flag,
I think it is a matter of individual self-esteem and national pride to have a capital which reflects the character of all Canadians from coast to coast.
That, Mr. Speaker, is basically what the hon. gentleman is proposing in this legislation, and basically what he has said over the years in trying to accomplish his objective. He is saying to us all that we do not as a whole understand exactly why he has been proposing to amend Section 16 of the Constitution Act, 1867 that the national capital of Canada become designated as the national capital area. It is a fact of life today that Parliament, that the federal Government, has expanded to the Quebec side. The National Capital Region itself includes municipalities on both sides. Why not make it the capital of Canada? He is also saying that there will increased co-operation between municipalities. He is making the accusation that this area is presently, and I will quote him exactly, " . .. the most over-governed and over-taxed region of Canada." He said it is so because of a total lack of co-operation between various levels of government, local and provincial. He makes the point that it is a simple matter, and something for Government to think about, to amend Section 16 of a simple Order in Council. He is not saying that he is trying to get rid of Ottawa.
I commend the hon. gentleman for his persistence and perseverance on behalf of his region and on behalf of his constituents. I believe that, regardless of what happens now, we will see in the not too distant future the Hon. Member's proposition become a reality.

Mr. Speaker, before embarking upon the comments I have prepared for this debate today, I should just like to make a few comments on the remarks which have just been made by the Hon. I wonder if he knows what Parliament is, Mr. Speaker. Later on in his remarks, the Hon. Member said that the federal Government had expanded its operations across the river. I believe that is probably what he meant. I hope he did not mean that Parliament has expanded in that way. I would suggest, therefore, that perhaps the Hon.

Member could be permitted to correct his first statement so as not to be on the record as having made a statement he did not intend to make with respect to Parliament expanding across the river, because, to my knowledge, Parliament has not.
1 am surprised, Mr. Speaker, that this Bill is now before us, that it was accepted by the Table officers. Presumably it was examined for legality before being presented to the House. I do not feel it would stand the test in the courts, with all due respect. If it became law despite its unconstitutionality- because I am satisfied it is unconstitutional-it would be tested in the courts of the land. I am sure of that. Even the most recent constitutional documents which eventually became the Constitution Act of 1982 provide adequate justification for my comments. 1 can go back earlier than that to the British North America Act of 1867 where again there is a provision suggesting that this is an unconstitutional document.
It has been brought to us, Mr. Speaker, improperly and I intend to demonstrate that. I will choose the most recent document, which of course is not the law of the land, and look at this particular Bill against the background of the Constitution of 1982, as I must. This is a Bill which has to mesh or be found not to mesh with that particular Act. I draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, to Part V, Section 38(2) of the Constitution Act of 1982 wherein the following is found, and I will paraphrase it in order to make it a readable sentence: An amendment made under subsection 1 that derogates from the proprietary rights, or any other rights or privileges of the legislature, or government of a province, shall require resolution supported by a majority of the Members of each of the Senate and the House of Commons, and, Mr. Speaker, the Legislative Assembly is required under subsection 1.
You will notice that the wording of this particular Bill before us, which was presented by the Hon. Member for Hull, purports to declare that the national capital of Canada, " ... shall consist...". This is a declaration of the House of Commons. Presumably, he would expect it to be declared also by the other place, otherwise it could not become law. But are we legally competent in face of what I have just cited, Mr. Speaker, to make any such declaration? I contend that we are not. We are acting beyond the powers that this particular Parliament of ours possesses under a law which was passed by this Parliament and approved by the legislatures of the provinces. I suggest to you, therefore, Mr. Speaker, that Bill C-206 is faulty, is before us improperly and is merely inviting a ruling by the Supreme Court of Canada to declare it ultra vires.
More than that, Mr. Speaker, the following is to be feared. I feel that legislation of this Parliament should be aimed at doing something positive to hold the country together. If one of the provinces were to contest this Bill before the Supreme Court of Canada, should it become law, the only result would be acrimony. Why are we considering a Bill which would produce acrimony in the country? Surely we have had enough of that. Legislation should not do that. I have suggested, as has the Hon. Member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), that
Constitution Act, 1867
this is more than invasion of provincial jurisdiction; it is an invasion of municipal jurisdiction.
The Constitution of 1982 has all sorts of appendices. One of them is what I still call the BNA Act of 1867. It describes the exclusive powers of the provincial legislature. One of them is property and civil rights. We are dealing with property here. This is incorporating the property of two provinces into a single unit. This is offensive to the BNA Act of 1867, Section 92(13). Property and civil rights are dealt with there and, to the best of my knowledge, that has not been withdrawn.
Section 92(8) deals with the exclusive jurisdiction of provincial legislatures. How can this Parliament dare-and I use the word advisedly-to consider legislation which derogates from Section 92(8) of the Constitution of Canada? It is invading a provincial jurisdiction by presuming to say that Ottawa and Hull are part of the national capital under the jurisdiction of this Parliament. That is absolute effrontery. The Member who proposed this Bill should have had the good grace to suggest that it would be expedient, once this Bill had been passed, to request the authority of the provinces to accede to the wishes of Parliament. However, this Bill purports to declare that something shall happen. There is nothing more affirmative than that. There is no concession or recognition that there is any other jurisdiction at all.
To whom would the residents of this capital pay their provincial tax? He had not thought of that, had he? The taxes in the Province of Quebec are a little high and people may not want to pay them in Quebec. Perhaps they could pay their taxes to the federal authority which now declares that this incorporated area is the capital of Canada rather than paying provincial tax. It worries me, Mr. Speaker, that we are considering a Bill beyond the powers of this Parliament to consider.
I would like to refer to Section 43 of the Constitution Act of 1982 which was proclaimed in front of this building. This Bill purports to amend the Constitution of Canada. I was surprised to hear the Member for Gander-Twillingate say there was going to be an Order in Council. This is now an Order in Council; this is a legislative Act being proposed.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first let me congratulate the Hon. Member for Hull (Mr. Isabelle) on his preparedness. You have explained why it is that for three Private Members' hours in a row we have been discussing matters concerning the National Capital Region, and particularly the constituency of Hull, that have been brought forward by the Hon. Member from that city. I guess it reflects upon the rest of us when we are not prepared for the eventualities of Private Members' Business under the new rules.
In the few minutes that remain let me address very briefly the constitutional issue which was touched upon by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), and gone into in some detail by my colleague from Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro). If we look at Section 16 of the Constitution Act, formerly the BNA Act of 1867, we find that the determination of the capital of Canada is stated under this section. It reads:
Until the Queen otherwise directs, the Seat of Government of Canada shall be Ottawa.
I think the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker) would have been quite right had his remarks referred to the situation 100 years ago when he said that strictly through executive action, through Order in Council, a change could be made. I strongly suspect that it is quite conceivable
that in those far off days the capital of Canada would have been changed fairly quickly.
I do not know why Ottawa was chosen. Maybe there were some military considerations, such as the existence of the military canal close by or the fact that Ottawa was a little farther away from the St. Lawrence River and the Great Lakes so it could not be readily attacked by our enemies then, now our friends south of the border. Perhaps it was another great Canadian compromise, having something right on the border between Canada East and Canada West as it existed before Confederation.
I suspect that there was a possibility that the capital might have been moved. It had been moved from Kingston and Montreal, if I remember correctly, in times past. As years went by things have changed. If one looks at the remarks of Mr. Justice Cartwright in 1966, in the Munro versus National Capital Commission case, one can see that his interpretation at that time, some 20 years ago, was that the authority, prescribed by Section 16, of the Queen to change the location of the seat of Government of Canada would now be exercisable by Her Majesty in right of Canada, and that while the section contemplates executive action, as cited by the Member for Gander-Twillingate, the change could doubtless be made by an Act of Parliament in which Her Majesty acts with the advice and consent of the Senate and the House of Commons of Canada. At that time it was suspected by the Supreme Court that the change could not be made by executive action alone but that it would require an Act of Parliament to make the change.
Since that time we have had the Constitution Act of 1982. I think that constitutional traditions and constitutional conventions have developed in the intervening period to the point where right now we would be satisfied with the arguments made by the Hon. Member for Esquimalt-Saanich that to change the capital would indeed be a constitutional change requiring the consent of the provinces.
To get away from the technical constitutional arguments, let us take a wider view. The Bill we have before us addresses itself to the question of the location of the capital of Canada. If we have that in mind, why can we not at the same time consider other possibilities than the present location? One hundred or more years ago, this was the centre of the population of Canada, the centre of the wealth of Canada. There was very little to the West at that time.
Things have changed in 100 years. The West is built up. Before there was only Prince Rupert Land. Now there are cities like Vancouver, Edmonton and Calgary. This is where the rapid growth in population has been. This is where the new wealth of Canada has been created over the years. Why can we not now look at the possibility of changing location to a place that is approximately at the geographical centre of Canada? I am not suggesting that we necessarily go to Gimli, Manitoba, but we might at least look at the possibility of moving to Winnipeg. It would be a lot easier for western Members of Parliament to go to Winnipeg than it would be to take a plane to Toronto, then change planes in Toronto and
February 24, 1984

come to Ottawa. As years go by and the make-up of the House of Commons changes, as it should do, that argument will become more and more relevant.
Another series of problems that we have with Ottawa as the capital of Canada is that this is very much a company town. The one industry here is Government. This gives rise to all manner of problems. There is no cross-fertilization of ideas between people who are principally involved in government and people who are principally involved in business or some other endeavour. For that reason I think sometimes the decisions made in Ottawa, in the comfortable ivory towers in the capital city, do not reflect the thinking of Canadians who live elsewhere in this country. It is not right when there is an isolation of the people who do the governing from those who are governed. I think there is a lack of knowledge on the part of many people in Ottawa, especially those who work in the

Government Departments here, pertaining to the real life of Canada and Canadians.
If we were to buy this argument, then we might want to move the capital of Canada to a place like Toronto.
